title: Fair Ranking as Fair Division: Impact-Based Individual Fairness in Ranking

problem.claim: Rankings allocate exposure and economic opportunity to ranked items, raising fairness concerns.

gap.claim: Relevance-linked exposure fairness can rely on difficult-to-defend link functions and still produce unfair rankings.

contributions.claim: Axiomatic ranking fairness framework rooted in fair-division principles that quantifies impact beyond exposure without requiring a link function.
Fairness axioms requiring envy-freeness and dominance over uniform ranking for every item.
Ranking objective related to Nash Social Welfare for computing policies satisfying the proposed axioms.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The proposed solution has guarantees for envy-freeness, dominance over uniform rankings for every item, and Pareto optimality.
Conventional exposure-based fairness can produce substantial envy and disparate impact on items.
Empirical illustrations show how the framework controls the trade-off between item fairness and user utility.

narrative_sequence.summary: Rankings are central interfaces whose positions allocate exposure and economic opportunity.
Existing fairness approaches link exposure to relevance, but the link may be hard to defend and may remain unfair.
The paper introduces fair-division axioms and a Nash Social Welfare-related objective for fair ranking policies.
The proposed solution is reported to guarantee envy-freeness, dominance over uniform rankings, and Pareto optimality, while conventional exposure fairness can create envy and disparate impact.
The framework is empirically illustrated as controlling the trade-off between item fairness and user utility.

source_observation.claim: Fairness can be formulated through allocation principles rather than a chosen relevance-to-exposure mapping.

interpretation.claim: When a fairness link function is contestable, axiomatic allocation criteria may provide a more defensible abstraction.

application.claim: Use item-level allocation axioms to design ranking policies when exposure alone does not capture impact.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish how the framework performs across specific domains, datasets, or deployment constraints.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the optimization procedure or computational complexity.
The abstract does not report datasets, baselines, numerical results, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not define the precise impact measure beyond its relation to exposure.
The abstract does not establish independent verification or reproducibility.
